title: I Belong to Glasgow
description: Dundee-born music-hall comedian Will Fyffe said he wrote this tipsy anthem after a cheerful drunk talked to him at Glasgow Central Station. Its chorus, “Glasgow belongs to me,” is still sung in the city’s pubs a century on.

title: Rock Island Line
description: Lonnie Donegan, the “King of Skiffle,” was born in the East End district of Bridgeton in 1931. His sped-up take on Lead Belly’s railroad song set off a craze for washboards and tea-chest basses that put guitars in the hands of the young Beatles.

title: Shout
description: Lulu, born Marie Lawrie, was 15 and living in the tenements of Dennistoun in the East End when she belted out this Isley Brothers cover. It went Top 10 in Britain, and she has been closing shows with it ever since.

title: The Jeely Piece Song
description: A child in a new tower block can’t get a jeely piece (a jam sandwich) thrown down from the 20th floor. Folk singer Adam McNaughtan’s comic protest about the 1960s high-rises is pinned here at the site of the Red Road flats, demolished in 2015.

title: Delilah
description: Rock showman Alex Harvey grew up in the Gorbals, the tenement district on the south bank of the Clyde. His band turned Tom Jones’s murder ballad into a stomping piece of theatre, and their live recording reached the UK Top 10.

title: Blue Boy
description: Edwyn Collins’s band made this jangling single for Postcard Records, run by Alan Horne from a tenement flat on West Princes Street. Postcard’s “Sound of Young Scotland” gave British indie music a template for the decade.

title: Waterfront
description: Jim Kerr’s band sing about the Clyde riverside on this bass-driven anthem, and filmed its video at the Barrowland Ballroom, the old East End dance hall that became the city’s favourite rock venue.

title: Tinseltown in the Rain
description: Paul Buchanan and Robert Bell met as students at the University of Glasgow before forming The Blue Nile. This string-swept single from “A Walk Across the Rooftops” turns a wet night in the city into something cinematic.

title: Dignity
description: Ricky Ross’s band sing about a council road sweeper saving up to buy a little boat he’ll call Dignity. It is pinned at the City Chambers on George Square, the grand Victorian headquarters of the council he works for.

title: The Concept
description: Teenage Fanclub came out of Bellshill, a town on Glasgow’s eastern edge whose 1980s guitar scene became known as “the Bellshill Sound.” This six-minute opener of “Bandwagonesque” fades out on a long, harmony-laden coda.

title: The State I Am In
description: Stuart Murdoch’s band recorded their first album, “Tigermilk,” as a project for the Electric Honey label run by music students at Stow College. This wry, confessional opener began a cult that grew well beyond Glasgow.

title: Why Does It Always Rain on Me?
description: Singer Fran Healy was an art student at the Glasgow School of Art, Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s building on Renfrew Street, when Travis took shape. This rueful hit about bad luck and grey skies made them one of Britain’s biggest bands.

title: Take Me Out
description: Before Franz Ferdinand, Alex Kapranos booked bands at the 13th Note, a vegetarian café and basement venue on King Street. The band’s tempo-shifting breakthrough single was nominated for a Grammy and took Glasgow art-rock worldwide.

title: Geraldine
description: Glasvegas come from Dalmarnock, an East End district by the Clyde. Singer James Allan wrote this wall-of-sound ballad in the voice of a social worker, and sings it in his own unvarnished Glasgow accent.

title: The Mother We Share
description: Glasgow synth-pop trio CHVRCHES, led by singer Lauren Mayberry, a law graduate of the University of Strathclyde, broke out with this bright, glassy debut single. It set up a career of stadium tours and festival headlines.
